items.item: Why a varint's own continuation flag is a genuinely data-dependent branch and not something a decoder could know in advance from the list alone
Why a single outlier forces an entire frame-of-reference block to a wider width, never just the one value: a block has exactly one stored width for everything in it
Why patching a handful of exceptions aside costs far less than widening a whole block to fit them, and why that trade only pays off when outliers are rare
Why separating the control stream from the data stream changes nothing about the bit budget but everything about whether a vector instruction can read the data as one contiguous run

items.item: Why this topic's own measured list shows frame of reference costing more bits than plain varint — a real, outlier-driven result on this particular list, not a universal ranking of the two schemes
Why decode speed is reported only from the papers' own named hardware in this topic, never from a Python timing — interpreter overhead would hide exactly the branch counts the topic is about
That the Roaring array container from the previous topic is literally the plain sorted list this topic starts from — the two topics' own running examples connect directly, not just by analogy

Why a frequency block benefits from patching while a document-delta block does not, in Lucene's own postings format — a real production instance of exactly this topic's own patching-versus-not trade-off

That the counting floor computed here (log base two of the binomial coefficient) is the exact same style of argument Chapter 1 and Chapter 12 each used for their own structures, applied now to a sorted list rather than a filter or a comparison tree
